analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling in the Atlantic Ocean and Gulf of Mexico.
analysis.headline: A one-sponsor bill to permanently ban Atlantic and Gulf offshore drilling was referred to committee and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Corrine Brown of Florida proposed amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Interior Secretary could never lease any Atlantic Ocean or Gulf of Mexico waters for oil or gas exploration, development, or production. The ban would have been permanent and would override any other law on the subject. It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts, especially in Florida, whose beaches, fishing grounds, and tourism economies would be shielded from the risk of a major offshore oil spill. Commercial and recreational fishing interests would keep waters free of drilling infrastructure. Taxpayers would avoid exposure to spill cleanup costs, since federal law caps some industry liability for offshore spills.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, tourism, and fishing communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas anywhere on the outer Continental Shelf of the Atlantic Ocean or Gulf of Mexico [S2][S3].
The prohibition is written to apply notwithstanding any other provision of law, so it could not be undone by a later leasing plan or executive action — only by a new act of Congress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to future Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico drilling acreage, and the nation would forgo whatever domestic production and federal royalty revenue those areas might have yielded. Coastal states would give up potential revenue-sharing from offshore leases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers, plus forgone royalty revenue

drawbacks.text: A permanent ban forecloses all future domestic oil and gas production from the Atlantic and Gulf outer Continental Shelf, reducing potential energy supply and the federal and state royalty revenue that leasing would have generated [S2][S3].

The bill takes an all-or-nothing approach: rather than case-by-case safety review or buffer zones, it prohibits every lease in two vast regions permanently, which critics of drilling bans argue is too blunt a tool even granting spill risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's upside was protection for coastlines and coastal economies from the kind of catastrophic spill that dominated the news when it was introduced; its cost was forgone energy production and royalty revenue, and the permanence of the ban left no room to revisit the tradeoff as technology and circumstances change. Weighing that honestly, the largest gains would flow to coastal communities rather than to any concentrated interest, while the costs would be diffuse — a modest share of future energy supply. It was, however, introduced with zero cosponsors and never advanced, so its design was never tested in committee or debate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Corrine Brown of Florida introduced the East Coast and Gulf Coast Ocean Protection Act of 2010 on May 12, 2010 [S1][S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources; two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies interested in future Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico leases are better off, since the shelf remains open to leasing decisions under ordinary law rather than a permanent statutory ban. The status quo of congressional inaction on offshore drilling protection also persisted.

for.name: Rep. Corrine Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently bar oil and gas leasing on the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico outer Continental Shelf.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action after sending the bill to subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape beyond its single Democratic sponsor cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production companies
industries.note: The bill would permanently erase the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico outer Continental Shelf from future leasing, removing drilling acreage these companies could otherwise bid on. Because their gain under the status quo comes from access to public waters — with spill risks borne by coastal communities — their interest here runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

A permanent leasing ban would keep drilling activity out of Atlantic and Gulf waters that support beaches, charter fishing, and seafood harvests, so the industry's interest tracks with the coastal public's. The bill never advanced, so nothing changed for them.
